sections.title: H1, standfirst and the answer up front

fields.label: Standfirst
paragraphs: An O-ring is described by two numbers — inside diameter and cross-section — and by at least four numbering systems that express them differently. This guide shows how to read each one, how to convert between them, and how to measure a ring when you have the part but not the paperwork.
leads: inside diameter and cross-section
marked: An O-ring is described by two numbers — **inside diameter and cross-section** — and by at least four numbering systems that express them differently. **This guide shows how to read each one, how to convert between them, and how to measure a ring when you have the part but not the paperwork.**
fields.note: 51 words · the two-numbers framing is the whole subject, and it makes the four standards feel like notation rather than four different products

fields.label: The answer block <h2>

lines: How do you identify an O-ring size?

parts.text: Measure the inside diameter and the cross-section — the thickness of the rubber. Those two figures identify the ring in every system. On an imperial drawing they appear as an AS568 dash number, such as −214. On a current metric drawing they appear as an ISO 3601-1 code giving the inside diameter and cross-section directly, for example 24.99 × 3.53. BS 1806 is the older British imperial series and has been superseded by BS ISO 3601, though legacy drawings and spares lists still quote it.

fields.note:
85 words · a complete answer with a worked example in each system and the supersession stated in the same breath.
“The thickness of the rubber” is deliberate — “cross-section” is the correct term and half the people searching this do not know it yet

notes: The H2 is the query. “How to identify an O-ring size” is the head term for this topic and it is a question, which is the format that gets lifted.
Self-contained, 60–90 words, no anaphora. It has to survive being quoted alone.
Two worked examples inside the answer — a dash number and a metric code — so the passage is useful without the tables below it.

sections.title: Reading an AS568 dash number
sections.chip: The table the meta description promises

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: An AS568 dash number is not arbitrary. The first digit group sets the cross-section; the rest counts up through inside diameters at that cross-section. So every −2xx ring is the same thickness of rubber and they differ only in how big the hole is. Once you know the series, you know the thickness without a chart.
leads: The first digit group sets the cross-section; the rest counts up through inside diameters at that cross-section.
marked: An AS568 dash number is not arbitrary. **The first digit group sets the cross-section; the rest counts up through inside diameters at that cross-section.** So every −2xx ring is the same thickness of rubber and they differ only in how big the hole is. **Once you know the series, you know the thickness without a chart.**

fields.label: Table

parts.text: The full series runs from −001 to −475, 369 sizes in all. Take −214: the 2 series fixes the cross-section at 0.139 in (3.531 mm), and 14 is its position in the inside-diameter sequence at that thickness. Half the identification is done before you look anything up.

sections.title: ISO 3601 — the current standard, in three parts
sections.chip: 🛑 Absent from the live page entirely

fields.label: H2
lines: ISO 3601: the standard current drawings cite
fields.value: ISO 3601: the standard current drawings cite

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: ISO 3601 comes in parts, and a drawing may reference more than one of them.

Part 1 — inside diameters, cross-sections, tolerances and designation codes. This is the size standard. It defines two tolerance classes: Class A, the tighter one, and Class B, the standard one. Class A size codes correspond to the AS568 dash numbers, which is the bridge between the inch and metric worlds and the single most useful fact on this page.
Part 2 — housing dimensions for general applications. The groove, not the ring. Squeeze, groove width and depth, and how full the groove is come from here.
Part 3 — quality acceptance criteria. Which surface imperfections are allowed and how large they may be.

A complete O-ring specification usually references all three: the size from Part 1, the groove from Part 2, the acceptance grade from Part 3. A drawing that gives only a size has specified a third of the part.

sections.title: The two British series

fields.label: H2
lines: BS 1806 and BS 4518: what to do with a legacy drawing
fields.value: BS 1806 and BS 4518: what to do with a legacy drawing

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: BS 1806 is the British imperial series, and it was widely used before ISO 3601 replaced it. It covers the same cross-section groups as AS568 plus a number of sizes that fall between AS568 sizes — which is why an old British drawing occasionally calls for a ring that has no AS568 equivalent at all.
BS 4518 is its metric counterpart, giving sizes as a metric inside diameter and cross-section rather than as a dash number.

Both have been superseded by BS ISO 3601, and neither should be specified for new work. Both are still worth knowing, because spares lists outlive the drawings they came from and a machine built in 1985 is often still running. Send us the old number and we will identify the ring; where the size has no modern equivalent we will make it to the original dimensions.

sections.title: Measuring a ring you already have
sections.chip: The highest-intent section on the page

fields.label: H2
lines: How to measure an O-ring you already have
fields.value: How to measure an O-ring you already have

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: Most people arrive at a size chart holding a part, not a drawing. Measure the cross-section first — the thickness of the rubber — with a vernier or a micrometer, gently. Then measure the inside diameter, laid flat on a surface, without stretching it.

Three cautions. A ring that has been in service is not the size it was made. It may have swollen in the fluid, in which case it measures large; it may have taken a compression set, in which case the cross-section measures flat on two sides. Measure a spare if you have one, and if you do not, say that the sample is used.

Second: an O-ring has a circular cross-section. If the part in your hand is square, rectangular or has a lip on one side, it is not an O-ring — it is a quad ring, a square-section seal or a rotary shaft seal, and it is specified a different way.
Third: measure the groove too. The ring tells you what was fitted; the groove tells you what should have been.
leads: Measure the cross-section first
Three cautions.
Second: an O-ring has a circular cross-section.
Third: measure the groove too.

sections.title: The groove is half the specification

fields.label: H2
lines: The groove is half the specification
fields.value: The groove is half the specification

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: An O-ring does not seal because of its size. It seals because the groove squeezes it — the ring is compressed between the groove floor and the opposing face, and that compression is what closes the joint. Get the groove wrong and a perfectly correct ring will leak.

Three things have to be right. Squeeze — too little and it does not seal, too much and it takes a set or extrudes. Groove fill — the ring swells and expands with heat, and the groove must have room for it; a groove filled to capacity has nowhere to put that growth. Surface finish — a scored groove or a rough opposing face abrades the ring, particularly where it moves.

ISO 3601-2 gives housing dimensions for general applications, and the figures belong there rather than in a rule of thumb. Take the groove from the standard, or send us the application and we will work it with you — the numbers vary with static or dynamic duty, pressure and compound, and a single quoted percentage would be wrong more often than right.

sections.title: Quality grades — and one honest exclusion
sections.chip: 🛑 ISO 3601-3 covers aerospace; Margo does not

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: ISO 3601-3 classifies the surface imperfections an O-ring may carry and sets limits on them — flash, parting-line projection, back rind, flow marks, non-fills, indentations, blisters and cracks. It sorts them into grades: Grade N, the general-purpose standard of acceptance; Grade S, for optimum-performance industrial and aerospace applications, with tighter tolerances and fewer allowable imperfections; and Grade CS for the most critical service.
Most industrial work is Grade N, and specifying above it costs money for no benefit. Ask for Grade S when the consequence of a leak justifies it, not by default.

One exclusion, stated plainly. ISO 3601-3 is written to cover aerospace O-rings as well as industrial ones. We do not supply aerospace — that requires AS9100, which we do not hold. We hold ISO 9001:2015, certificate 09111526A, Integral Certification Ltd, valid to 21 February 2027, scope: rubber moulded components, and we are upgrading to IATF 16949, targeted by the end of 2026.
